Arabia
a-rā'bē-ä
n. (the great desert country south and east of Palestine, whose kings brought tribute to Solomon, whose merchants traded with Tyre, and in which Paul places mount Sinai)
From Hebrew 'Arab, connected with 'arabah, a desert plain or steppe, and with a root meaning to grow dark — hence the waste, the evening land. The Authorized Version also renders the people Arabians and speaks of “the mingled people that dwell in the desert”.

Biblical Definition

Arabia in Scripture is not a nation with a throne but a vast tract of tents, flocks and caravans, whose chiefs are called kings and whose wealth was mobile. In Solomon's day it paid: “And all the kings of Arabia and governors of the country brought gold and silver to Solomon” (2Ch 9:14). Ezekiel lists it among the trading partners in the great lament over Tyre: “Arabia, and all the princes of Kedar, they occupied with thee in lambs, and rams, and goats: in these were they thy merchants” (Eze 27:21). Isaiah lays a burden on it and pictures the caravans driven off the roads into the scrub: “The burden upon Arabia. In the forest in Arabia shall ye lodge, O ye travelling companies of Dedanim” (Isa 21:13), and Jeremiah sets “all the kings of Arabia, and all the kings of the mingled people that dwell in the desert” (Jer 25:24) among the nations that must drink the cup. In the New Testament the name carries the whole weight of an argument. Paul, contending against the Judaizers, writes: “For this Agar is mount Sinai in Arabia, and answereth to Jerusalem which now is, and is in bondage with her children” (Gal 4:25). Sinai stands outside the land of promise, in the desert, and the covenant given there gendereth to bondage; the Jerusalem above is free. Paul himself went into Arabia after his conversion (Gal 1:17) and returned to Damascus, and the years there are the silence out of which the apostle to the Gentiles came.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Arabian and Arabic; in sacred history Arabia is the desert country south and east of Judea, whose kings brought gold to Solomon and in which mount Sinai stands.

expand to see more

ARABIA, n. A large country of Asia, lying south and east of Judea, chiefly desert.

Its inhabitants dwelt in tents, kept flocks, and conducted the caravans of the east.

All the kings of Arabia and governors of the country brought gold and silver to Solomon.

The princes of Kedar traded with Tyre in lambs, and rams, and goats.

The apostle Paul states that mount Sinai is in Arabia, and thither he went after his conversion.

Key Scripture

2Ch 9:14 — "Beside that which chapmen and merchants brought. And all the kings of Arabia and governors of the country brought gold and silver to Solomon."

Isa 21:13 — "The burden upon Arabia. In the forest in Arabia shall ye lodge, O ye travelling companies of Dedanim."

Eze 27:21 — "Arabia, and all the princes of Kedar, they occupied with thee in lambs, and rams, and goats: in these were they thy merchants."

Gal 4:25 — "For this Agar is mount Sinai in Arabia, and answereth to Jerusalem which now is, and is in bondage with her children."

Modern Corruption

Galatians 4 is now widely read as an allegory that Paul invents and that carries no doctrinal weight. Paul offers it as the true sense of a real history, and the two covenants he distinguishes there are the hinge of the whole epistle.

expand to see more

It is common to hear that Paul's Hagar-and-Sarah passage is a rabbinical flourish, an ingenious allegory that a modern reader may admire and set aside. That reading takes shelter in the word allegory and ignores what Paul does with it. He does not treat Hagar and Sarah as figures rather than women; he treats two historical women, two historical sons and two actual mountains as bearing a covenantal meaning that God intended when the events happened. Sinai is in Arabia, outside the land, and the covenant made there could not give the inheritance. That is not decoration; it is the argument by which he tells the Galatians that circumcision under the law will make them debtors to the whole of it.

The doctrine at stake is the distinction between law and gospel, and the Reformed confessions guard it because everything else depends on it. The law is holy, just and good, and it cannot justify a sinner; “the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith” (Gal 3:24). Flatten Paul's Arabia into a literary device and the two covenants blur into one continuum of religious effort, which is precisely the error the epistle was written to kill. The desert where the law was given is still a desert; the Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'Arab (H6152), Arabia; 'arabah (H6160), desert plain, steppe; 'ereb (H6154), the mingled people; Greek Arabia (G688); Sina (G4614), Sinai.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'Arab (H6152) — Arabia; the desert country of the east and south.

Hebrew 'arabah (H6160) — desert plain; the terrain behind the name.

Hebrew 'ereb (H6154) — a mixed multitude; the Authorized Version's ‘mingled people’.

Greek Arabia (G688) — Arabia; where Paul went and where he places Sinai.

Greek Sina (G4614) — Sinai; the mount of the covenant that gendereth to bondage.

Usage

"“All the kings of Arabia and governors of the country” — desert chiefs paying tribute to Jerusalem."

"“The burden upon Arabia” — the caravans driven into the scrub by war."

"“This Agar is mount Sinai in Arabia” — a geography turned into an argument about covenants."
